prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and international trade shape labour demand, wage structure and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B006 as a single part, credited to Autor, Hanson and Katz. I rechecked it because ten of eleven files now name the same set, and that convergence is not evidence of merit. I tested it against the common criteria. First, novelty and conceptual content: the skill-demand and task framework gives an account of how technology changes labour demand, and that account can be taken to data. Second, credibility of identification: the local-labour-market designs for import competition separate exposure from outcomes more transparently than most observational work in the shortlist. Third, maturity: the skill-premium work is about three decades old, the task framework over two decades, and the trade-shock papers over a decade, with replication, extension to other countries and sustained criticism. The open points concern the size and persistence of the effects, not whether adjustment costs exist. Fourth, breadth: the work is used in trade, macro, public economics and the policy debate on adjustment. As a growth and structural-change economist I see its value in measuring how labour actually reallocates across tasks, sectors and places, which is the margin my own field mostly assumes. I count that as field proximity, not as additional merit. On the chair's Katz-or-Dorn question, I keep Katz because the citation is built on two linked strands. One is the long-run supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and wage structure. The other is the evidence on trade exposure and local adjustment. Autor spans both and Hanson carries the trade-shock design. A fixed Autor-Dorn-Hanson set would be the cleaner single-discovery prize, and I would accept it if the committee decides the trade-shock evidence is the achievement. I would not drop to Autor and Hanson alone, because that discards the framework that makes the evidence about labour demand and not only about local adjustment. The citation should name what was shown, avoid claiming origination of the whole task framework, and avoid restating the 2023 and 2024 citations.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weakest part. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is excluded by the cap, and Levy, Murnane and the task-model contributors lie outside the credited names. Katz's best-known education-technology work was with a recent laureate, so his marginal credit is the most exposed in the trio. The three-person set may read as two lines, technology and trade, joined by a shared outcome and not as one discovery. The persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects, and shift-share inference, are not fully resolved. The 2023 and 2024 prizes are thematically adjacent. I judge that to be a timing and wording issue, not prior recognition of this discovery, but I could be wrong about how much it weighs. If the committee gives priority to a single separable mechanism with clean credit, B004 or B007 could look tidier. I still find B004's attribution worse and B007's identification weaker.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B007 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) for its clean credit and breadth. He would credit only Autor and Hanson in B006, treating Katz and Dorn as adjacent and Acemoglu's earlier recognition as a complication.
responses.response: I agree that B007 has the cleaner attribution and a mature, unified programme, and I do not dismiss it. The disagreement is partly about evidence. The theoretical and organising contribution is strong, but the headline results on constitutional and electoral-rule effects depend more on specification than the design-based evidence in B006, and your own case names this as the main weakness. I also read the Autor-Hanson pair differently. It credits the trade-shock and task evidence and drops the skill-premium account that frames it. If the committee wants a narrower prize, I would sooner swap Katz for Dorn than shrink to two names. I would revisit B007 if the later quasi-experimental work you mention carries its main empirical claims, and not only its theory.

responses.point: Strömberg asks whether B006 is one coherent discovery or two lines. He calls Katz's marginal claim, given the work with a recent laureate, the most exposed part of the trio, and offers Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the fallback within the same discovery.
responses.response: I think it can be framed as one discovery: how exposure to technology and trade changes labour demand and distributes adjustment costs, tested with credible designs. It cannot be framed that way if the wording drifts into claiming the task theory or the education-technology race. I agree that Katz's separate credit has to rest on his wage-structure and skill-premium work, not on the Goldin collaboration, and that this is where the committee should push. I accept your fallback as defensible. The test I would apply is whether a citation that names only local adjustment to trade is as informative about labour demand as one that includes the skill-demand framework. I think it is somewhat less, and that is the only reason I keep Katz.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) keeps B006 as his preferred prize but says Katz is the weaker fit for the trade-shock strand. He would accept Dorn for Katz if the committee decides the trade-shock evidence is the core, and he keeps Katz for the framework that makes the trade evidence interpretable. He now treats B032 as a strong but narrower alternative.
responses.response: We agree that this is a judgement the committee should test, not a settled point. I would add a criterion. The case for Katz is stronger the more the citation is about wage structure and labour demand, and weaker the more it is about local adjustment to import competition. So the choice should follow the citation wording, and the wording should be fixed first. On B032, I take your revision as reasonable. The mechanism is foundational and its attribution is clean, but the evidence is indirect and the 2022 prize narrows the room for it. I do not rank it above B006 on the common criteria.

responses.point: Teorell flags adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes, doubts whether technology and trade are one coherent achievement, and says Katz is the closest call within B006. He accepts that a narrower trade-shock configuration may be right if the combined citation is too loose.
responses.response: I agree that these are the real threats to the case. On adjacency, I read the earlier prizes as recognising different discoveries, so I would treat it as a matter of how the citation is worded and what the committee wants to say it adds, not as a reason to discount merit. On coherence, my test is whether the citation can say in one sentence what was learned about labour demand and adjustment without listing the two channels separately. The wording I propose attempts that. I share your view that the Katz and Dorn question is the committee's closest call. If the committee cannot agree on one sentence, that is evidence for the narrower trade-shock set, and I would then support Autor, Dorn and Hanson over Autor, Hanson and Katz.

responses.point: Krusell moved B006 to first on the merits. He discloses a connection to Persson (B007) and field proximity to the skill-premium strand through his own capital-skill complementarity work. He keeps Katz over Dorn because Katz anchors the long-run framework, and treats B007 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I accept your reasoning that Dorn's exclusion follows from the cap and not from a weaker contribution. I also note that you are among my closest collaborators, and your disclosed proximity to the skill-premium strand and my own field proximity should be weighed in the same way. Neither of us should rely on the other's agreement as a check. I would put it to the committee that the case for Katz must stand on his distinct wage-structure work and not on our shared view of the task and skill-demand literature. I am less certain than you that Dorn's claim is secondary, and I would not want the cap to settle a question the evidence leaves open.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name. This depends on whether the citation covers wage structure and labour demand broadly or local adjustment to trade only, and on how much of Katz's credit survives the overlap with the recent laureate.
Whether the committee reads technology and trade as one discovery, and whether one citation can say so without claiming origination of the task framework or restating the 2023 and 2024 citations.
How far shift-share inference concerns and the persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects should weigh on maturity and on the wording of the citation.
Whether the 2023 and 2024 prizes should lower the marginal case for B006 on timing, even though I judge them to recognise different discoveries.
Whether the near-unanimity in round 1 reflects independent assessment on the stated criteria or movement toward the leading option, which I cannot determine from the files.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose long-running collaborations and IIES colleagueship with Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair), including co-authorship with both. Both support B006, so their agreement with me should not be counted as independent confirmation of my view. Krusell has disclosed a possible Persson connection on B007, and Teorell's field is adjacent to B007. I note these without adjudicating them. My regular co-authors Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. My field proximity to growth, structural change and labour reallocation is disclosed, and I have applied the same criteria as for other fields. I am an Associate Editor at Econometrica and Quantitative Economics. That role is not a tie to any shortlisted candidate. I have not independently verified any source beyond the supplied evidence.
